newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain's Telefonica seen ready for more competition.
newsitem.headline: Spain's Telefonica seen ready for more competition.

text.p: Spanish telecommunications firm Telefonica has whipped itself into shape for the market's upcoming liberalisation, establishing a pre-eminent position from which it is expected to face tough competition.

The once unwieldy mammoth, which until 1992 took six months to install private phones, has implemented profound changes over the past two years. Analysts consider it will be fit for full privatisation in 1997 and foreign competition in 1998.
"Telefonica is well positioned for the coming liberalisation and in the next few years it will maintain its advantages over its competitors," said Ignacio Cornejo, analyst at Beta Capital.
The market has taken notice, sending the group's shares soaring more than 70 percent since the beginning of 1996 to a new record high on Tuesday morning of 2,885 pesetas.

Telefonica announced last week it had overhauled its board, drastically reducing its size and changing the members. Analysts saw this as the latest step in a transformation which began in 1994 under former chairman Candido Velasquez.
Juan Villalonga was named chairman last June after the new centre-right government came to power.
"The overhaul of the company board was more political. It's normal that a chairman would prefer to people in key positions people whom he can trust," said an analyst at Ibersecurities.
"The restructuring in which shareholders are more interested started two years ago and the new managment is continuing with the same philosophy," he said.
Telefonica's first competitor, mobile operator Airtel, started out in October 1995. Now Retevision is set to be privatised and to become Telefonica's domestic competitor in basic phone business.

The government has said it plans to sell its remaining 21 percent stake in Telefonica early next year, although it will retain some authority through a "golden share" allowing special voting rights on strategic issues over a ten year period.
But Telefonica has yet to address its tariff structure, before it is ready to confront competition.

"At present, Telefonica is subsidising local calls with revenues from international and long distance calls. But with the upcoming liberalisation it can't go on doing that," said an analyst with a Madrid brokerage.
"The adjustment of tariffs to real costs is very slow, and until this is completed, the company will not be ready for a completely liberalised market," he said.

For the past year, Telefonica has reduced its long-distance tariffs by 25 percent, but still suffers competition from foreign "dial-back" systems which return calls from abroad to take advantage of cheaper foreign rates.
Analysts said a change in Telefonica's tariff structure should help the group's revenue.
"Short-distance calling demand is more rigid than that of long-distance and international calls, so the likely increase in long-distance demand should increase total revenues," said one.
He added that a more open market like those of the United States and Britain should also prove advantageous for Telefonica, with the consequent growth in consumption.
Telefonica has not suffered from changes so far, reporting a 19.8 percent rise in net profits to 120.23 billion pesetas ($934 million) in the first nine months of this year. ($1=128.7 Peseta)
